utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed, though Mr. McCloskey is on his feet, that the Defence would have a preliminary matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. If I could, this will just take a moment. You'll recognise we have a new person. This is -- we're lucky and privileged to have Melissa Pack with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Welcome in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We should address one topic according to your guidance. We have to address the topic of the witnesses that the Prosecution does not have questions for and we offer them as 92 ter witnesses, and our position is that the fact that the Prosecution does not have questions for these witnesses does not change their status. And we tried to discuss how to solve this problem, and we think that the best way is to have those witnesses via videolink at one point on -- in time when we have other videolink witnesses, so it could take only ten minutes since there is no additional questions and just attestation of the statement. So I -- since we have to have them viva voce attest their statement. It's not possible to have it in writing, so we have to find some other ways, and we think that's the only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say since we have to have them in viva voce attest their statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's true for 92 ter witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not for 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but we do not want to change the status of our witnesses because of the fact that Prosecution does not have questions. We still intend to keep those witnesses as 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what's -- why is that? I mean, you limit yourself to having a statement in evidence to which the witness has attested either 92 ter, that he comes to court and says, "What I said is the truth," or there's a written short statement that said what I said is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours would accept that it can be done in writing form and still we have 92 ter witness, then we do not have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But why should they be 92 ter? I mean, what's the difference exactly? Of course, there are a few matters; 92 ter witnesses can talk about the act and conduct of the accused. If that's the issue, then I understand that you say, We can't present them as 92 bis witnesses because the subject matter of their testimony does not allow us to present the witnesses as 92 bis witnesses. That's something I understand. But in general statements, we present them as 92 ter, therefore they should remain 92 ter under all circumstances, that's something I do not understand yet what the -- what interest is served by that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I understand, 92 bis witnesses should support some other evidence. They cannot stand alone. And 92 ter witnesses, in my understanding, are more of -- of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's a very short summary of which I would say some of it is -- represents what the -- what is both in the Rule and in the case law. First of all, Rule 92 bis does not exclude anything but gives some -- it gives factors which are in favour of admitting in evidence in a written form. And certainly it's true that it says if, for example, it's one of these six elements we find in Rule 92 bis (A) which certainly are in favour of admitting, whereas there are also factors against admitting. But it is still for the Chamber to decide whether or not apart from the strict rules that it should not go to prove -- of a -- of the act and conduct of the accused. I mean, that's clearly explained in Rule 92(A) in the start of that article, but all the rest is a matter of weighing and considering to what extent there are factors in favour or factors opposing such an admission. But that's different from what you are telling us now. You say 92 ter witnesses should remain 92 ter witnesses. If they meet the standards here, you could consider whether or not to present them as 92 bis witnesses. Again, I'm not saying that ... One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, having very briefly communicated with my colleagues, I would like to make two observations. The first is that, of course, if I say the witness has to write down that he told the truth, that should be in the presence of a court officer. I mean -- but, as you may know, you can ask for someone to be appointed as a court officer. You could also try to take them all together and have one court officer taking all these attestations. That's one. Second, there's also a suggestion, but I don't know whether I understood you well, that the probative value of 92 bis witnesses would be lower than 92 ter witnesses, and that would also be true if there would be no further examination or cross-examination of those 92 ter witnesses, which means that only the statement is there and we see a face of a person who says, All I said is the truth. No further questions. That's it. Well, there the Chamber might well disagree, if that is what you want to tell us, that the probative value is different. Under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still, it's different if the other party has the opportunity to question and challenge something from the statement and they actually choose not to, then it's of course different from telling the other party that they do not have right to cross-examine because it is 92 bis witness as we see before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if a party says I'm not going to use my right to cross-examine, then it's that party - in this case, the Prosecution - who says: I have that right, I'm not going to use it. So why should you then insist on offering an opportunity to exercise a right which they announced they would not exercise?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do not understand why the other party when they choose not to cross-examine our witness, why that change the status of our witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a simple matter of concern about efforts. It's a concern about everything where there's no difference in substance. There is no difference in substance in this specific situation between a 92 bis and 92 ter statement apart that we do not see a face which doesn't say more than I attest to what is put on paper. We don't see that face but we read that in the presence of a court officer that person has said so and has signed for it. Now, to bring witnesses here is a costly matter which we -- I think the Tribunal gladly accepts if there's any difference in substance to the witness not appearing. Our question is: What is the difference? Again, I see the point: If the witness is talking about act and conduct of the accused, that's a good legal reason to bring that witness to The Hague. But in general to say if the Prosecution doesn't want to cross-examine the witness, that doesn't make any change. We'll bring that witness to be here with us for two minutes and to say exactly what he could have said to a -- to a presiding officer appointed by the Court, that's what we still do not understand. And we have a task in trying to be as efficient as possible both in terms of time but also in terms of finances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am afraid that I was misunderstood. I didn't offer to bring the witnesses here. I offered to have videolink --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even that may be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's very low cost. One of them live in the same city where the videolink would be held, so there is no travel cost, there is no stay costs, there is no any kind of costs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's certainly changes slightly the situation, although your basic argument was we are not going to change the status of 92 ter witnesses. Even then, but that's still not entirely clear to the Chamber on what basis you make such a statement. But I think there is no disagreement that hearing those witnesses through videolink certainly saves some of the expenses we would have if the witnesses would appear here in The Hague. That is, I think, commonly understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would hope so, although I don't know the cost the Registry incurs going there and all, unless you're talking about it being part of a regular 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that Mr. Lukic already made clear that he would combine it with a testimony given through videolink which, for other reasons, has to be organised anyhow. So that certainly is well understood, Mr. Lukic, that that saves time, saves money. But the basic argument was 92 ter should remain 92 ter and that is something the Chamber does not understand yet. We do understand that the costs involved would certainly be less if it would be combined with a videolink testimony that will be conducted anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to put your fears at rest, Mr. Lukic, I don't agree with you that a 92 bis witness's testimony, it is only supportive of other evidence. If it is dealing with a particular situation and it's the only evidence on that, that's the only evidence and it's as strong as any other evidence. That it has not been cross-examined doesn't make it any weaker. It's not cross-examined because the opposite doesn't cross-examine it, they agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour is probably waiting for my answer to your observation. But having read some previous judgements, I think that there might be some differences, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let me -- it's, of course, a matter to -- still to be discussed on if you accept the testimony of a witness, does not always necessarily mean that you would agree with the substance of all of it. But the decision not to cross-examine is because the Prosecution thinks that putting further questions to that witness would not assist its case. If a witness comes here and gives only sweeping statements without any basis for it, I could imagine that the Prosecution takes the position that sweeping statements are not statements about facts which are identified as such, and that therefore there's no need to cross-examine a witness if he doesn't bring any facts and therefore there are no facts to be challenged. That's all. Why the Prosecution does not cross-examine the witness is entirely to be decided upon by the Prosecution itself. That's the situation. And we are comparing the situation where there's only a written statement plus an attestation, either 92 ter in court or through videolink or in written format under Rule 92 bis, and that there's nothing else, and what we'd like to do is to save as much time and to save as much money as is possible and still guaranteeing a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to add that I don't think that the Prosecution does not have cross because of sweeping statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I just gave a possible example. They could think it's not relevant and therefore there's no use to cross-examine the witness. They could think that these -- it's not about facts because -- and therefore there's no need to cross-examine the witness. They can give -- I don't know, I'm not talking about any of these statements. But there may be many reasons why you would or would decide not to cross-examine a witness. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, those are all good examples of reasons why we would not. One thing that is clear is by not cross-examining we're not agreeing to anything in the statement. If we choose to agree, we can agree, but by not cross-examining we are not agreeing to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the practice of this Tribunal pushes the parties if they do not agree they have to cross-examine and they have to challenge what they do not agree with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a total misunderstanding. If one party presents totally irrelevant evidence, there's no need whatsoever to cross-examine the witness and to say that what is irrelevant was different but if it's still irrelevant, we shouldn't spend time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why do you suppose that our witness is irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not supposing anything. But the Prosecution, they have, I think, 400 witnesses, and on some of them they have decided that they would not cross-examine for one out of the many, many reasons a party could have not to cross-examine a witness, and Mr. McCloskey just said, well, for example, relevance, whatever, and of course they are bearing the consequences of that. Because if -- let's just assume that testimony - and it would work the other way exactly the same - if you have not challenged evidence which is not relevant, if you make a mistake and if it turns out to be relevant, then you may be in trouble. But that's for the parties to consider. I take it that if the Prosecution decided not to cross-examine the witness, that they'll accept that that is what the witness presented as evidence, and what role that evidence plays or what weight to be given to it, that's for later is for argument. And the fact that you always have to cross-examine witnesses if you disagree with the substance of what the witnesses tell us, that's a total misunderstanding of the system, I would say, more in general terms of the common law traditional system and certainly what is the practice before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With all due respect I have to disagree, Your Honour. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- a party has to present its case and has to challenge everything that goes against its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the evidence goes against its case. Now, it could well be - and again, don't blame me for just choosing one of the many, many possibilities - if a witness would come with unsubstantiated evidence, then it -- that party, the opposing party, may consider that evidence which doesn't go against its case because it's not concrete. If evidence is presented which is not relevant, the party could say, Well, it doesn't go against my case because it's irrelevant for my case at all. If it goes about all kind of details where the party considers that the details are not part of their case but it's the core of the testimony, and even if details are different, that they don't have do put their case on irrelevant details, that's all for the parties to decide. But I emphasise that party will bear the consequences of its assessment and will bear the consequences of its -- of the attitude of the procedural approach they've taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours asked us to give our position how to solve this situation, and we gave you our position so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we want you to reconsider that in view of apparently -- of what we just discussed, and we do understand that at least as far as costs are involved that you want to accommodate that concern by adding them to existing -- adding them to videolink testimonies that will be conducted anyhow. That's clearly on the record. And the Chamber appreciates that at least that matter of the costs has caught your attention and that you have given it thought how to accommodate that. It does not, however, resolve the apparently existing in the Chamber's wrong understanding by the Defence of the duty of a party to cross-examine. I think we leave it to that at this very moment. Then, Mr. Lukic, since we are dealing with some other matters as well, you're also due to give us an update on expert reports. The matter has been addressed on the 26th of January, and the matter has been addressed again on the 2nd of February, where the last words I spoke were: "Without going into details now, could you please consider whether you could, on shortest notice, give us whatever information you have or perhaps even not have yet but which you understand the Chamber would need." That is about the expert witnesses. To say, well, they're not ready yet is not the kind of information -- well, it's the beginning of the information we need. They're not ready yet. Then we want to know when they will be ready, when will the reports be there. That's -- and you have had at least some time now, a week, to further verify what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we postpone this -- our address until the end of this day, working?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait until the end of this day and hear further from you. Meanwhile, the witness can be escorted into the courtroom and I used the time -- Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is just one matter before the witness is brought in which is that he should be advised of his rights under Rule 90(E). He was so advised in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, as a matter of fact, Mr. Lukic, having read the statement that -- that there certainly is reason here to give the witness a 90(E) warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. I shall take the liberty of asking you to caution the witness before he begins with his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I will do. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time to bring the following -- to put the following on the record. On the 19th of January of this year, the Defence e-mailed the Chamber and the Prosecution stating that it had received and uploaded a revised translation for Exhibit D727 to which the Prosecution has agreed, and the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the existing translation of D727 with the revised translation, which is uploaded under doc ID 1D17-0327.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petrovic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. It's now handed out to you by Madam Usher. Could you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Petrovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. But before he starts his examination, I'd like to bring the following to your attention. Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal state as follows: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question and testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." That means that you, as a witness, if you think that the truthful answer to any of the questions might incriminate yourself, that you can address me and seek that you'll not be under an obligation to answer that question. We'll then decide whether or not we require you to answer that question. But please be aware that if you have not asked me not to answer a question, then you should give a truthful answer. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Stojanovic will now examine you. Mr. Stojanovic you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As is the customary procedure here in the courtroom, could you please give us your exact name as slowly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mile Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, at one point did you provide a statement in writing to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have 65 ter 1D01674 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you have a screen before you and you can see the statement. On page 1 of this document, you can see a signature. Once you've seen this, I would kindly ask you to tell the Court whether that is your signature.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask that we look at the last page of this document, 1D01674.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, on this page of the document, can you also recognise your signature? And the date that you can see on this page, is it written in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask that we look at paragraph 8 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, while we were preparing for you to appear in this courtroom, did you indicate to me that a correction should be made here; namely, in the first sentence instead of the word "in front of," and then it says "under the flat roof of an unfinished house," it would be right to say "under the flat roof of an unfinished house"?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I don't understand what you are saying. I don't see "in front of" in this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It comes a few lines later. But in the first sentence, there was already "under the flat roof of an unfinished house."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, not "in front of."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the B/C/S version, it says: "In front," "ispred." So the difference is only in B/C/S and that's why the witness asked us to correct the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well then, now the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- original statement then is the same as what we find in the, until now, wrong English translation and now the accurate English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, once we've corrected the B/C/S version of your statement, today, in this courtroom, now that you have taken the solemn oath to tell the truth and nothing but the truth, would you give the same answers to the questions that were put to you while this statement was being taken?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And these answers, would they be your best recollection and your best knowledge regarding everything that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender 1D01674, the witness statement of Mile Petrovic, so that it could be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01674 receives Exhibit D894, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I would like to read the summary of Witness Mile Petrovic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Mile Petrovic was a member of the VRS during the war in BiH, and in July 1995 he was within the platoon of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade. In that period, he was often absent from the unit because of the health problems that his newborn daughter had, so he was not aware of any activities of his unit around Srebrenica. He remembers that sometime in July 1995 in the town of Bratunac he encountered Momir Nikolic, then a captain and chief of intelligence and security affairs in the command of the Bratunac Brigade, who had previously ordered him and the commander of the military police platoon, Mirko Jankovic, to take a military APC together him and go to Konjevic Polje. As they were moving down the road towards Konjevic Polje, somewhere before that, they were stopped by two men who were searched on Nikolic's orders and brought into the APC. The assumption was that these Muslims who were leaving Srebrenica. Upon arriving in Konjevic Polje, they handed over these prisoners to a soldier who they found in front of an unfinished building after Nikolic had interrogated them. The next task that he received from Nikolic was that, together with Jankovic, who was driving the APC, they take two members of UNPROFOR towards Bratunac, which is indeed what they did, but at the request of these persons, they went around the road towards Bratunac for about 2 kilometres and then they returned to Konjevic Polje. The witness points out that he is aware of the testimony of Momir Nikolic during which he presented many untruths. He says that Momir Nikolic is absolutely not telling the truth when he mentions him as a person who killed six prisoners on that occasion. In addition to that, Petrovic testifies about other untruths that were then stated by Nikolic. Finally, he says that he is aware of part of Nikolic's testimony, stating that he had reported to General Mladic in Konjevic Polje. He claims that on that day they did not see or encounter General Mladic and his escorts on that day either in Konjevic Polje or along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. That is the summary of Witness Mile Petrovic's statement, and with your leave, I would just like to put a few questions to him in order to clarify certain matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please take a look at paragraph 5 of the statement that is now D894.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I just wanted to try to get the chronology right here, if possible. This is what you say in paragraph 5: "We set off from the compound of the Bratunac Brigade towards Konjevic Polje ..." I would like to ask you to try to remember, if you can, and tell the Trial Chamber, to the best of your recollection, can you say what part of the day it was when you set out from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I think it was in the afternoon. The actual time, I really cannot say. I mean, I cannot say exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "in the afternoon," I would like to ask you to try to tell the Trial Chamber whether this was the evening afternoon hours or earlier afternoon hours?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. We had returned from Konjevic Polje. It had been day-time for quite a while. We didn't spend much time there. It was day-time when we were returning from Konjevic Polje. It was well into the day. It could have been, say, I don't know, say, 1.00 onwards, 12.00, 1.00, onwards, I don't know the exact time. However, I know that when we were returning, we were well into the day. It wasn't late or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. In order to assist all of us here in this courtroom to understand your testimony, in paragraph 6 and paragraph 7 you speak about your activities in Konjevic Polje. Can you assess, to the best of your recollection, how much time you spent in total in Konjevic Polje from the moment when you arrived when you spoke to these prisoners -- actually, the interviews conducted by Momir Nikolic, then taking the UNPROFOR men, and then going down the road or up the road to Bratunac, and then after that going back to Bratunac? How long did all of that take?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean from Bratunac, when we left Bratunac for Konjevic Polje, or how much time we spent in Konjevic Polje itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please. Could we take this step by step. Please tell us how much time you spent in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: In Konjevic Polje, we spent about an hour and a half or two there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm going to end with the following question. According to your knowledge of the area and that road and the possibilities of that APC, how much time did you need to get to Konjevic Polje from the command of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how fast an APC goes. It's 21 kilometres from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje. Now I don't know exactly. I don't want to tell a lie or anything. I don't know exactly how it takes an APC to get there. The driver was not very knowledgeable either. He didn't really know how to drive it. It was the first time that he entered a vehicle like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us any time-frame, to the best of your recollection, for these 21 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it certainly takes more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At this moment we're not going to put any more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for the time allocated to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters missed what Mr. Petrovic said when Mr. Stojanovic had thanked him. Mr. Stojanovic said: "Mr. Petrovic, thank you." What did you then say, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Petrovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Pack. Ms. Pack is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll find her to your right. Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you may recall I cross-examined you before in the Karadzic case. In your statement at paragraph 12, and there's no need to look at it, you'll remember you take issue with Momir Nikolic's evidence that six Muslim men surrendered to you on the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje and that you told him at Konjevic Polje that you had killed them. You say that there were only two Muslim men and you didn't execute them; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: There were two Muslims, and I didn't kill them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You take issue with Mr. Nikolic's evidence that you told him at Konjevic Polje that you took revenge for your brother; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You agree you had a brother?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He was killed during an ABiH attack on Bjelovac, where you were from, on 14th December, 1992. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were with Nikolic on one occasion at Konjevic Polje on the 13 July; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we look at your statement at paragraph 1, please. That's D894. And if we can just have it on the screen. Page 2 in the B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In July 1995 you say, I'll just read it: "I was engaged as a conscript and assigned to the post of a military policeman in the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac. There was a military police platoon in the Bratunac Brigade and its commander was Mirko Jankovic and his superior was Captain Momir Nikolic, chief of the intelligence and security organ. There were about 20 of us military policemen in this platoon." What you don't state, of course, in that first paragraph of your witness statement is that you were a commander, weren't you? You were deputy commander of the Bratunac Brigade Military Police Platoon in July 1995. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there. I was just told, and that's what I said before. I don't suppose I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You've been asked about this before, and I'm going to remind you of your testimony at Momir Nikolic's sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 31975, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I've difficulties in matching the answer with the question, whether the witness was anywhere or what his function was, of course, are two different things. So therefore before we move on, could we verify that the witness has understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You understand the question. Were you deputy commander of the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was not officially appointed. No papers were made to that effect. I was just told that if Mirko Jankovic was away, I would be standing in for him. However, since Mirko was there all the time, there was no need for me to deputise for him. I just did my usual service as -- as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, you've had trouble with this before. Can I ask you, please, to turn to --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 31975 on the screen, page 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll read it out. It's in English, so I'll read it slowly. From the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we have in B/C/S on our screen apparently is something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Something else. Yes. It's another part of the package but not the transcript. This is the transcript of the sentencing hearing when this witness first testified in 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This document only exists in English, Witness. Therefore, carefully listen what is read to you and we'll verify whether that is what we see on our screens. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. "Q. Mr. Petrovic, were you the deputy commander --"

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's line 16, I apologise. For Your Honours, line 16. "Q. Mr. Petrovic, were you the deputy commander of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, yes or no? "A. I was not given a document. I was just told orally by Nikolic that I was to stand in for Mirko when he wasn't around. "Q. May I take your answer as meaning, yes, that you were the deputy commander of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade. "A. Yes. But there was no order to that effect. "Q. Mr. Petrovic, did you de facto perform the duty of deputy commander of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade in July 1995? "A. Yes."

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, it was not the brigade commander. It was the commanding officer of the military police platoon. You keep saying "brigade commander." I was the commander of the military police platoon, and I was appointed verbally. You can think of it what you like, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you would accept, wouldn't you, that your commander Mirko Jankovic understood that you were his deputy. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Jankovic was not a commander. He was a "komandir." And if I was his deputy, I didn't have a written appointment for it. The only thing I was supposed to do was to stand in for Mirko Jankovic in the military police platoon if and when he was absent.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll just turn to the next page, 17, in your testimony in the Nikolic sentencing hearing. Line 21. You were asked: "Mr. Petrovic..." And this is what the questioner said to you. "... I will read part of the interview of Mr. Mirko Jankovic..." It's in the B/C/S and it goes on: "... where Mr. Mirko Jankovic says the following: "'My name is Mirko Jankovic and by rank I am a sergeant, but it says here that I'm a sergeant first class. I don't know how come. This is a rank I had in the civil police while I was working in the military police."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Turn over the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And please read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "'The next person was my deputy and that was Mile Petrovic.'" And you were asked: "If Mirko Jankovic says you were his deputy and you're saying you weren't, does that mean he was lying or, rather, not telling the truth?" You answer: "He was telling the truth. I told you. I got this orally. And I don't know -- how I do know how he [sic] understood this way or that?" Just to fully understand, you accept Mirko Jankovic was telling the truth when he said you were his deputy; right.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was a deputy by oral orders. It was -- I was just told I would deputise for him, but it was not an official written appointment. That's the problem. You don't distinguish between an oral and a written appointment. When you appoint somebody in writing to a certain duty, that's one thing. And it's quite another thing if we are sitting in the room together and Momir Nikolic says, "You'll be standing in for Mirko if he goes away." What kind of appointment is that? You were able to see that before and after that I did guard duty, I went out into the field to bring commanding officers into custody, et cetera. A commander doesn't do any of these things. All of us who were in the military police, we obeyed orders. We obeyed what we were told. You are trying to represent me as a deputy. I'm telling, Mirko -- Nikolic told me to deputise for him occasionally, but I wasn't officially ap pointed as a deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, unless it has some specific importance for what now follows, I think the positions are pretty clear that you are --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. The witness apparently feels the need to emphasise that he was not formally - that is, in writing --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- appointed. Let's move on and see what the relevance of this dispute is for anything that comes up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were promoted to commander of the military police platoon, just to finish this, of the Bratunac Brigade in March 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: In March?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the mobilisation. I stayed on in 1996 when Mirko Jankovic was relieved of his duties because of his age. It was after the Dayton Accords; right? In 1996. After older men began to be dismissed from the army. Is that the period you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be -- if this is a convenient time. May be time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, I was checking something else. It is a convenient time for a break. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I was just -- my attention was diverted slightly because on page 24, line, 16 I'm interested as Dr. Falke, or -- no. I think as a matter of fact it was Judge Fluegge who was introduced as such. I can testify that Judge Fluegge is not a medical doctor nor he is Dr. Falke. That's why I missed your question, whether it was an appropriate time for a break. It is. We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, perhaps in -- in follow-up on what we discussed earlier, could I invite you to carefully read Rule 90(H) where the -- 90(H)(ii). There is a specific obligation for the cross-examining party who uses cross-examination not exclusively in relation to the subject matter of the evidence in-chief and matters affecting credibility of the witness but also uses cross-examination to put questions relevant to the case for the cross-examining party itself, if it uses cross-examination in that way and if then the witness, answering those questions, is giving evidence which is in contradiction of the cross-examining party's case, under those circumstances an obligation arises that the nature of the case of the cross-examining party should be put to that witness. But that only arises if the witness is cross-examined, that's first; second, if that cross-examination is used to elicit evidence which is not linked to the subject matter of the examination-in-chief but, rather, relevant to the case of the cross-examining party, and only then if the witness contradicts that party's case under -- only in -- if these three requirements are fulfilled, the obligation arises to put the case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a short analysis of Rule 90(H)(ii). Ms. Pack, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you know Nadin [phoen] Blagojevic yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you see him on the 13 July on the road or at Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's not in your statement but you've said before you also take issue with Momir Nikolic's evidence that you used a megaphone on the 13 July to call upon Muslim men to surrender. Do you still dispute that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I do. I never called on anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You agree with Nikolic that you travelled on the 13th July in an APC from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I travelled with him and Mirko.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mirko Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This was a stolen UN APC; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It was white and it had UN marked on it in big black letters; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You agree that Muslim men were called upon to surrender by Bosnian Serb forces using megaphones. This was along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. That did happen?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw the civilian policemen talking into a megaphone. In fact, I don't know if it was the radio from their car or a megaphone. I saw them as we were passing by.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You agree the Muslim men were given ultimata. They were told it was safe, that they would be exchanged on the megaphones?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I couldn't hear from the noise of the engine what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The evidence in this case is that Muslim men were deceived into thinking that it was indeed safe for them to surrender because they saw an UN personnel carrier on the road. That was your intention, wasn't it, you in the APC, to deceive the Muslim men into thinking it was safe? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Perhaps Momir Nikolic knew that. But as we were going from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, along the road we saw 50 to 100 men who had come down even before we had arrived at that point. They had already surrendered. They only asked us to give them water, and I threw at them water in -- in Tetra Pak that I found in the APC.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You don't deny that that's what happened, that Muslim men surrendered because they saw a UN APC along the road?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I just told you, as we were coming to that point, those people had already come there. They were already there. As we were moving towards Konjevic Polje, we were running into them along the road, and they were asking for water. And I went with those two members of the UN. Up there, people had also been asking for water. They were carrying some other people on stretchers --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll ask you about the UN men in a moment. You know that these men, these Muslim men who came down to the road, save for a very few who escaped, you know they were executed by Bosnian Serb armed forces on the 13th and in the days after that. You know that's the case? You accept that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that day, nobody was executing anyone as we were driving from the APC from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje and back. I didn't see any of that. I only saw them coming to the road. And as they were coming, there were some people already there along the road, on both sides of the road, and whether some more people came later I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On the night of the 13th July, this isn't in your statement, Muslim men and boys were detained in Bratunac in buses and trucks lining the streets and at various locations. You know that?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Bratunac Brigade military police were amongst those guarding them. You know that?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On the morning of the 14th July with your commander, Mirko Jankovic, you escorted the convoy of Muslim prisoners which travelled from Bratunac to Zvornik; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: We drove the APC. I think it was also on the 14th, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The stolen UN AP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Ms. Pack. Could you please also answer to what is the core of the question and not just in the margin of it. The question was whether you escorted the convoy of Muslim prisoners. And then you say: "We drove the APC." When driving the APC, were you escorting a convoy of Muslim prisoners on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does "escort" mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means to accompany a group of Muslim prisoners, and you can do that in many ways, apparently it's suggested to you that you did that while being seated in an APC, whether you were there to keep an eye on Muslim prisoners, a larger group, going to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had received orders to accompany those not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't ask whether did you it on orders or not, but I asked you whether you did it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we accompanied those trucks and buses to Zvornik. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. D00285 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps this will help you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have, please, in the English page 14, B/C/S page 17. This is the Bratunac Brigade military police daily log-book. You've seen it before. Look at the entry, please, dated 14th to 15th July. "The police was engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees." This entry describes your escort of the Muslim prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thousands of Muslim men transported from Bratunac to Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. All of that was in that convoy. In trucks and buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You driving in a stolen United Nations APC; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was not driving. Mirko Jankovic was driving.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: These men whom you led escorted to Zvornik were executed by members of the VRS, starting that day on the 14th, apart from a very few survivors. You know that's what happened; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I heard all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's go back to the 13th July, please. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Paragraph 8, for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You don't need to look at it. I think you'll remember. When you were at Konjevic Polje, you say Momir Nikolic told you to give two UN soldiers a lift towards Bratunac; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not to Bratunac, but as far as they want to go, take them there, and when they want to return, you return them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. Just to I can fully understand your evidence, you say you didn't take these men -- well, let me understand this and you can tell me whether this is correct. You didn't take these men to anywhere in particular. You just took them for a ride back down the road towards Bratunac and back again. That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, took them, brought them back.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just to take them for a ride in your stolen UN APC; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You left Momir Nikolic at the Konjevic Polje intersection, the cross-roads, you left him there?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Both of these soldiers, these Dutch UN soldiers, have given statements to the ICTY. Going to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking, no speaking at an audible volume. The rules are clear. Mr. Mladic, one more word aloud and you'll know what the consequences will be. And please, it's not the public gallery that you are -- have to stay attention to but rather to what happens in this courtroom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: These Dutch soldiers. I'm going to read you an extract from the statement of one of them, Martijn Mulder. It's an ICTY statement taken in October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have it on the screen. It's 65 ter 31980.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before this document leaves the screen, it's not -- is it the Prosecution's position that the witness was part of this police that escorted the people to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. And I think he testified that he was a passenger in the United Nations APC that travelled from Bratunac to Zvornik on the morning of the 14th July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But not that he was one of those listed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, he's not on that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, that's -- his name isn't amongst that list, but he indeed confirmed that the police were engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- and that was what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. You were about to read from the statement given by one of the Dutch soldiers, which we have not yet on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And actually perhaps I may assist His Honour Judge Moloto just with the previous exhibit. But that page, under the heading "Reception," there was a list of names. As I understand it, those names are of those of military police that were on duty that day there Bratunac in that location. But not the list of those who were escorting the convoy from Bratunac to Zvornik. I hope that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still need the B/C/S version of this statement. Yes. Could you identify the pages to the extent you've not done that yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, of course. B/C/S page 12 and the English page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed that we only have seven pages in this document. Could you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'll check myself as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies. Perhaps I've got it -- yes, I do apologise. It's page 4 in the English. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S, Your Honours, it's also page 4. I do apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And just while that's coming up, let me just ask you this just to finish up on the last exhibit. It's not in front of you now. But the list of names for 14th July, those were the men who were on duty, right, in Bratunac on the 14th July, the list that you saw there. Is that accurate, do you recall, in the previous exhibit? I can bring it up again, but if you can't recall it ...

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was here, just now?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, in fairness, I should bring it up because that way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness referred to what he saw. The short list handwritten you saw a minute ago, any question about that? Ms. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't read it. I just saw that it says desk something.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honours in fairness I should do it because His Honour Judge Moloto asked. I just would prefer if I -- if I do put it to the witness, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please get it back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. If we can just go back to the prior exhibit. It was D00285. And we're just asking for pages 14 in English, 17 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And then we'll go back to this document I'm showing you now. Let's just deal with these names here. Can you see the names? The list there, under the heading "Reception."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have the wrong page again in -- we have English instead of --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in English, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's the wrong page as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's the wrong page in the B/C/S. There's the right page in the English, and the B/C/S will be coming up in a moment. Just to remind, it's page 17 of the B/C/S. And you have it there, 14 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we just go ... this is D00285, yes, that's correct, and we're going back -- not 17, it's page -- of the English it's page 14. B/C/S is page 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We'll get there. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just look under the heading, please, "Reception," and there's a list of names. Now you can tell me, you can confirm this, that that list of names is the names of those members of the military police who were then on duty in Bratunac; is that right? Yes? Under the heading "Reception."

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Is it separate from the police who were engaged in the escort of the Muslim prisoners; yes? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I guess so as long as it's written that way. If it's "reception," then they're at the reception.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope that clarifies. Sorry it took so long to get the exhibit up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although since you started speaking when the previous translation was still continuing, the beginning of your question is not clearly on the record. Could you perhaps repeat those words. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 36, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. And my -- first bit of my question: That's separate from the police who were engaged in the escort of the Muslim prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, therefore, the question was whether those who escorted the Muslim refugees are not necessarily the ones or even perhaps not the ones which are listed here, which as was put to you, were at the reception in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just know who was with me in this escort. Now, as for these persons it could have been some of them. Who knows? I mean, things turn out the way they are ordered. Now how can I say with whether somebody was there or not there. I cannot say anything for sure about anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can bring up the next 65 ter number, 31980. We're back on the witness statement of the Dutch UN member, and we're going please to the English page 4 and also the B/C/S page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see -- you can read while I'm reading this, you can read this statement yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: From the third paragraph in the B/C/S and the third paragraph in the English on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He says, describing his time to Konjevic Polje: "We then had to get into the APC and the soldier, who later went to sit on the commander's seat, told us to open the hatch of the APC and take our places at the top of the vehicle. He made this clear to us through hand gestures. He also told us in a mixture of English and Serbo-Croatian that we had to shoot at any Muslims. De Bruine and I were given a Kalashnikov each and we also got a flak jacket and a helmet. The APC then headed off in the direction of Potocari." These Dutch soldiers - this is my question - they sat on the top of the APC; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were not sitting on the APC and no one gave them any kind of rifle, and what you said just now, nothing, nothing, nobody forced them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You gave them a helmet, flakjacket?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: They found everything that was there. I didn't know where things were and I couldn't do anything. They knew the APC better than we did. They took what they wanted from the APC. They opened this cover, a double cover thing, and then they watched the Muslims who were coming --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, Witness, Witness -- could you -- Witness. One second, please. Could you please repeat what you said and speak slowly. You said: "They took what they wanted from the APC. They opened this cover, and they watched the Muslims who were coming ..." And could you please repeat what you said after that. So they watched Muslims who are coming and then what you did say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lady said that we gave them Kalashnikovs. I just had my own automatic rifle. I couldn't give it to anyone because I needed it. We were in danger, I and these two men, just like everybody else there. All the people who were there. But I haven't read all of this, so I cannot -- well, what it says here is that we forced them, something ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just divide it up. So they had helmets, blue helmets; yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I really do not remember. I swear. Whether they had blue ones or whatever. If they took it from the APC, then they may have. I cannot remember exactly what they had on their heads since they got out of the jeep.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And what you say is that they opened the hatch themselves and went up; right? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were not on the APC, they were in the APC.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone, says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please speak into the microphone. The usher will assist you in addressing. So don't speak too much in the direction of Ms. Pack but keep an eye on the microphone that the interpreters can hear you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm used to looking at the person that I'm speaking to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's fully understood. At the same time, we don't want to lose your words, your testimony, so therefore try hard to speak into the microphone. And perhaps it could even be a little bit more adjusted from here to the left so that there's a better chance that the sound reaches the interpreters. Yes. Ms. Pack [Realtime transcript read in error "Mr. McCloskey] if you would repeat your last question or put the next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I said Mr. McCloskey, but -- as it appears the transcript. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And what you say is that they opened the hatch themselves and went up, right, is that your evidence? That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because to tell you the truth, I didn't even know how to open it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'll read the next few paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we do so, are you telling us that in that stolen UN vehicle where you were armed that they just did what they wished to do and it was not under your control? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even consider them to be some kind of enemy. That's why I had no need whatsoever. I mean, if that's what you mean. I didn't consider them to be the enemy so that I would make them do this or that or the other thing. I mean, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I leave it to that. Please next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Next part of the statement: "About 1 kilometre after having left Konjevici and heading in the direction of Bratunac, the APC turned off the main road and drove directly into enemy woodlands where there were many armed Muslims." I'm just reading it. You can read it yourself. "We drove around that area for about 45 minutes, de Bruine sat on the top of the APC the whole time. So did I except for the last bit. "It would have been much better for our own safety to ride in the APC with the hatch down. Driving through the woodlands while sitting on the top of the APC was really very dangerous for us because we were acting as a target for the Muslims. There was no point in sitting on the top of the APC. It only made you vulnerable. "While we are driving around, the BSA gunner said that we had to point our weapons in the same direction as his 50 calibre. We did not see any Muslims and therefore we did not have to shoot." Question: You agree that these UN soldiers were in a vulnerable position sitting on the top of the APC.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, none of what you said just now is correct. Absolutely nothing. Except for that we went for a 1 kilometre up there. You say that had they seen Muslims and later -- I mean, had they seen them, they would have killed all of us from the road, Bratunac, towards Bratunac, from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. We did not turn off at all except for when they asked that we go back. No Muslims, no armed Muslims. They didn't see any. That's number one. Number two: We did not turn off the road at all and the ride did not take 45 minutes. Now, what else was it that we said? If you could take things one at a time and then I'll tell you, because right now I cannot remember all of that. And also, gentlemen, they were not on top of the APC. They were in the APC all the time. They were standing on those seats, like this. You see? So he could have lowered his head just like I could. I did not order him to do anything, and I didn't know how to. I didn't know how to say anything in English. I really don't know how to say all of this to you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what to say. All of this is not correct. We did not consider them to be our prisoners. We did not consider them to be some kind of enemy. As if I would be taking a ride with him just like that if he were my enemy, God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: You must understand that there was this man in the police, an Englishman. I don't know. When I brought him fish from my own children, he spent the night with us, slept with us, watched TV with us. Why don't you bring him to testify?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause there, please. Pause there, please. Now let's just go back to these Dutch soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to just bring up another statement if I may, 65 ter 31981, which is the last of the two -- the second of the two Dutch soldiers ICTY statement. Page 8 of the English, page 8 of the B/C/S. De Bruine. I'm just going to read one small extract. It's in the middle of the page in the B/C/S. Fifth paragraph down in the B/C/S. Bottom paragraph in the English at page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "We drove in the direction of Potocari. At one stage Mulder went and sat inside the vehicle." Well, let me just start with -- the preceding sentence will probably put it in context. "We were told to sit above armour and one of the fighters gave us flak jackets and helmets." Next paragraph: "We drove in the direction of Potocari. At one stage Mulder went and sat inside the vehicle. I stayed on top. When we had driven 500 metres from the junction, we turned down a side path. We drove around this area for about 20 minutes. The gunner instructed me to aim my firearm," that's the next page in English, "in the direction indicated by him. He said that there were Muslim fighters walking around there. I did not aim my fire-arm. About 20 minutes later, we arrived back at the T-junction. When we arrived back, one of the BSA fighters said that we had now taken part in a Serbian patrol. At this, the fighters laughed loudly." Does this jog your memory? You remember you or Jankovic saying something like this, finding this situation amusing with the Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, neither I nor Jankovic said that. This is not true. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me finally -- this is the last issue. Let me take you to the evidence of a witness, RM257, a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And I'd ask that what I'm going to ask to be shown is not broadcast. This is 65 ter 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's -- just not to look at the document or not to have even in open session the testimony of the witness referred to?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It can be referred to. It wouldn't reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's just simply not to go out as an abundance of caution. It isn't under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope -- it's not under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's not. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then it should not be broadcast. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 31998. It is not an exhibit in this case. It is the prior testimony of a protected witness in this case in other proceedings. Hence, my caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll read it out when it has come up. We want page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll read this slowly. He's asked, this witness: "From your position on that hill --" he's describing being in the woods along the road, Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. "Q. From your position on that hill, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you saw and heard? "A. From that position you could hear Serbs calling over loud-speakers for us to surrender. I saw an UNPROFOR personnel carrier with blue helmets on them, so we immediately recognised that this was the UNPROFOR. At one point, when they were calling out to us, they said, come down, don't be afraid. UNPROFOR is here to make it possible for you to be escorted to Tuzla. "Q. What did you decide to do then, sir? "A. Well, before we saw the UNPROFOR personnel carrier, nobody even thought about surrendering. I mean, why would we escape to the woods otherwise? But after this APC, it was my impression, well, the UNPROFOR is here, I don't think that they will kill us so easily. I thought that there was some hope, because I was tired and because of all the horrible things while crossing through the woods. I had then asked my father and my brother to go with me so that we can surrender. I think they gave us two ultimatums. One was at 12.00, and then the second one at 2.00 was when we decided to go down and surrender because the personnel carrier was constantly going up and down there to let people know that it was UNPROFOR, to impress that upon people better." Help me with this, please, Mr. Petrovic. Your purpose in driving up and down the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road in a UN APC with Dutch soldiers on top with their blue helmets on was to impress upon the Muslim men and boys in the woods that the UN were there, that they were safe; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: You'd have to ask Nikolic. He was the one talking to them. You understand? We just put them on the APC as we had been ordered. We drove them and we drove them back. Everybody could see that. Now what's written here, why would I make him go into the woods for 45 minutes? That way to Bratunac is just 2 kilometres. We went up there and returned. And even before, there had been hundreds -- or perhaps 100 Muslims already standing there who had surrendered. And those two UN soldiers, they could see when we started off from the intersection towards Bratunac, they saw me throwing water at the people. They saw the people asking me for help. They saw these people carrying others on stretchers, stepping on mines, and all those -- those two young men who were there, they could see it all. I didn't know anything. My job was only to drive those two fellows from the UN as I had been ordered and to bring them back. Now what Nikolic and they agreed between them, that's their problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question just as follow-up to the previous answer. For how long were you driving in the APC with the two UN soldiers in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 2 kilometres up and down. We drove slowly, as Nikolic told us, because they wanted to take a good look at everything. So we drove slowly for 2 kilometres and back. I don't know how long it took. Maybe it was the 45 minutes they mention. But that we took them into the woods, that's not true. Unless they think of that road as the woods. That’s how it was then… even the street was not as it should be, everything was pell mell. Maybe to them it seemed like the woods because there were woods on both sides of the road and that's why they thought that we were driving them into the woods. How would we dare to? We wouldn't dare because I was responsible for those two men while they were with me, and it was my responsibility to bring him back safe and sound. If Mr. Nikolic had entrusted them to me, I had to bring them back safe and sound, even if I -- if -- if it cost me my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One additional question. If it was your duty to bring them back safely, why didn't you do that right away instead of driving forth and back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wanted it. They wanted us to give them a ride. I don't know where exactly. I couldn't read their thoughts. And to bring them back when they were ready. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, you just -- sorry I -- thank you. I heard your answer. But they wanted to be carried back. But that is not what you did. You went forth and back with the APC carrier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. We only went up there. And when they told us to turn back, we turned back immediately. There was no going back and forth. I guarantee that with my life. We didn't go up and down, not even twice. We only went once and returned. They got off, got into their jeep, and left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And why, then, was it necessary that you drove the UN vehicle? They could have done that by themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. First of all, I wasn't the one driving; it was Mirko Jankovic. If they had wanted to drive the vehicle, of course they would have been allowed to. It was their vehicle. Maybe they were afraid. I don't know what they were thinking. But they didn't ask us to drive. If they had asked, why would I refuse? I wasn't the one driving. I couldn't even drive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
