utterances.text: I also have a few questions in this respect for you. The road from -- the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje is an asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier said that they may have been mistaken by being in the woods because it was not a proper road you were driving on. Do you remember that you told us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said there were woods on both sides of the road. When you go about 50 metres up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you said: "It was not really a proper road." That's what you said. And I'm asking you about that. Because I do understand that the -- the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road is an asphalt road. So what made you say that it was not really a proper road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a proper road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. I don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll verify that because you are recorded as having said when explaining that they -- it may have been the 45 minutes, which is pretty long for what you describe has happened, and that, as you said, they took them into the woods, that's not true. Because you said "unless they think of that road as the woods. It was not really a proper road." That is what you are recorded to have said. And do you want us to verify that? Because we have an audio recording of every word you spoke. So if you say, I didn't say that, we'll verify that. But if you said it, I'm asking you for an explanation as to why you said it was not really a proper road which, as a matter of fact, is more in line with what they said in their statements, more in line than with your statement that you just took the road and nothing else. Do you have an explanation for that or do you still want us to verify whether you spoke those words: "...it was not really a proper road"? Because then we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I didn't express myself correctly. What I meant was that it's not a really good quality road and that's why they might have suspected that it was a bad road along which we took them. That's what I meant. Otherwise, it's an asphalt road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. And there had been shelling along that road and maybe that's why I thought that it's not really a good road, like you have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you said "it may have taken 45 minutes." Now, if you drive at a very low speed, 20 kilometres an hour, for example, which is approximately the speed of a bicycle, then 45 minutes would cover 15 kilometres, which doesn't fit well in what you are telling us, unless you explain to us ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I said what I said. I don't know for how long the vehicle was moving, how long it took us to cover those 2 kilometres and drive back. That's why I stressed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you also don't -- do not exclude it was the 45 minutes, because what you said was "maybe it was the 45 minutes they mention."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what they said, that they were driving them around for 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on the road. Somewhere off the road. I'm telling you how long the vehicle was moving, there and back. I cannot properly assess the speed or how long it took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you accepted that it was possible that they were right in saying that it was 45 minutes. That's how I understand the line which reads: "Maybe it was the 45 minutes they mention." Do you have an explanation for accepting that for -- as a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps if you drive slowly those 2 kilometres, if it's possible that it takes 45 minutes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I maintain that we never went off the road anywhere. We didn't turn anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is only possible if you have an average speed of 3 kilometres an hour, which is difficult to imagine as the speed of such a vehicle. I have another question. You said: Of course, they could have driven the car if they had would have wished to do that. But you also testified that the car was stolen. Now, how to reconcile that the UN people were free to do whatever they wanted with that car, with that vehicle, and at the same time telling us that it was stolen, because if it's stolen that at least suggests to me that you've taken control of that, in this case, vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Nobody told us anything. Nikolic could have said, Give them the vehicle, let them take a ride in it. As for me and Mirko Jankovic, we had nothing against it. Whatever Nikolic ordered us, that's what it had to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what did he order you in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To have them get into the APC and give them a ride the way they wished: To drive them up there and bring them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he also say, Let them drive if they wished to and let them take the vehicle if they wished to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we didn't say that. We didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So allowing them to take the vehicle and allowing them to drive it themselves was not what was within your orders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Nobody was ordered us that. If they had, we would have done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then one last question. You've told us that what Nikolic said is all -- not true about this whole story. You also said: "I know that Nikolic presented many untruths in The Hague and made groundless accusations against other people." Could you tell us what other lies Nikolic would have presented here? So apart from this testimony, apart from this story about the drive in the UN vehicle, megaphones, et cetera. So apart from that, what other lies did he tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I killed those six people and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's part of this story. But apart from this story, did he tell in any other ways on other subjects any lies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, you mean overall, during his trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, during his trial, anywhere -- you said he told many untruths. So apart from, again, this -- these events, what else did he tell the Tribunal which was not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he lied about everything that concerns me, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. In relation to these events or in relations to other events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These events that we've been discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm exclusively focusing on other events where he may have not told the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That must be about something I heard in his testimony or statement that I've read. Maybe that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any specifics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember now when I was reading the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reading whose statement? Your own statement or the statement given by Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Momir's statement. I read his statement in a newspaper called the "Dnevni Avaz" when I first learned what he had said here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you did not re-read that statement in its original form at any later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But do I understand that all comments you give on Nikolic telling lies is based on what you read in newspapers only, not knowing exactly what he would have said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From his statement, as I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the newspapers? You never read any statement or any testimony by Mr. Nikolic apart from what you read in newspapers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You never saw any statement, apart from that. Then this takes me to another matter which is: Your statement was taken, you were interviewed in -- could you tell us exactly when that was? Or at least approximately when it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it a year ago? Was it in spring? Was it in summer? Was it in autumn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which statement do you mean? The one I gave to these lawyers here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I have given a number of statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The statements --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps a couple of months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember who interviewed you when a statement was taken for this case, the statement you attested to at the beginning of this session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A grey-haired man. An elderly man, grey-haired man. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when was that approximately? Was it more than a year ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was only a couple of months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And where was that interview held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you -- was it then put on paper what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was probably recorded. It was probably noted down in a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But was that done when you were interviewed or was that done later or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I answered whatever he asked me. I answered his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, I do understand that. Did they come to you twice or only once or three times or four times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once. Now, you signed the statement. Did you sign the statement immediately after you had been interviewed or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right after the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were interviewed, they wrote that down, and then you signed it. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read the statement and signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after you had been interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I put to you that - and it's -- it's not in my version, but I think the interview has been recorded as conducted in October 2013, which is far more than a year ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can have D894 again on the screen in both versions, especially the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, now, here it says that you signed your statement in June 2014, which is some -- some far less than a year ago. And it also states that the statement was taken in October 2013, so there is an interval of some eight months between being interviewed and signing the statement. Now, you told us a minute ago that it was all done on -- at the same occasion. Could you explain to us why you attested to this statement dated the 14th of October and signed some eight months later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I remember. I don't remember any different. 6 June that we see here; that's my handwriting and my signature. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, it states on the cover page that the interview was held in October 2013.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you said it was all on the same day, you may, Well, as a matter of fact -- or do you still insist that it all happened on the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I remember this last time. They came on the 6th of June, 2014, when I signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you give that interview before you testified in the Karadzic case, or did you give this interview after you testified in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After. Were there any things that bothered you in the Karadzic testimony which you then corrected or which you thought would need further explanation, or was the Karadzic interview -- Karadzic testimony, was that totally irrelevant for the statement you gave to the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber, Ms. Pack, does not know when the witness testified in Karadzic. Could you inform the Chamber about that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because you started -- well --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we should know -- January 2014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before -- Judge Moloto has a -- one or more questions for you. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, is it your testimony, really, that while you were in the middle of war, you came across two strange Dutch soldiers whom asked you to give them a ride and you just gave them a ride?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were there. We received orders to give them a ride. We brought them back. And I've already said everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but are you seriously telling us that that's the kind of order you got in the middle of the war: Give these men a ride, whom you didn't know, and bring them back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. To drive them there, bring them back, all of that. As I've said, all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to entertain them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's no entertainment there. People, there's no entertainment in war. You have to respect the individuals who are there. They were an international unit and whatever. They -- I mean, we did not feel that they were our enemies. They can also confirm that, who are heaven's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would have then one very short follow-up question. Talking about respect, which I appreciate, seems not to be fully consistent with stealing cars from them. Do you have an explanation as why you are so respectful to them and at the same time cars are stolen from them, or at least this car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? That vehicle that we brought, it's people from the field that brought that, and that vehicle was there and the police was guarding it. When Nikolic ordered to have this vehicle ignited, we didn't know how to do that. And Mirko Jankovic tried to get it going all day. Do you understand that? We are not the ones who stole the vehicle from these two men. This had arrived from the positions where there had been fighting. Do you understand that? And then it was brought there and it was left there where we were. And then we took over this vehicle the next day on the orders issued by the gentleman. We went there, and then we came back, and that's that. We're not thieves to steal vehicles. Who am I to steal a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said this had arrived from positions where there had been fighting. Do you know anything about under what circumstances the vehicle was stolen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I don't know. I wasn't up there. I don't know how all of that happened and whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether it was where there was fighting, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the vehicle was, say, in Jadar, up there, wherever, I don't know. I mean, how far away that is I don't really know exactly. Do you understand what I'm saying? That vehicle was brought from that area of the 3rd Battalion, where the area of responsibility of the 3rd Battalion was. It wasn't that we stole that vehicle, we policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have another follow-up question. Some minutes ago you said we had to respect the individuals who are there. They were an international unit. How do you knew that, that these two men were from an international unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they came in a UN jeep and they wore uniforms. That uniform that they had ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your statement, and I read it for you, you said: "As we drove towards Konjevic Polje, I cannot say exactly where, but I know that this was before Konjevic Polje. I noticed two men in civilian clothes as they came out from behind a small hill on the left side."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I withdraw my question at this point in time and come back to that later. I think we should take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break. Mr. Stojanovic, how much time would you still need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe about ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break now. We are late already. We take a break and will resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may before the witness is with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have short update on our expert witnesses. Demographer was filed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Demolition expert and military expert will be finalized until the end of this week, as it was announced. Ballistics expertise we already submitted to the Prosecution, only we have to arrange the numbers since the numbers are not correct for our case. And history expertise and communication expertise should be done in B/C/S before 14th of February, so in five days, and then we'll give it to the Prosecution immediately and we'll submit it for the translation. And we do not have any news for pathologist yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you at least for this update. Mr. Lukic, you may understand that most likely the Chamber will continue to push for anything we have not yesterday received or where there is unclarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll now -- Mr. Stojanovic, if you have any further questions for the witness in re-examination, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrovic, first of all, I'd like to ask you whether have you any personal knowledge about how this APC arrived in the command of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know at any point in time what happened to the APC later?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Except that we went to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 65 ter 31979 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, before you, you've got the second statement of the witness that the Prosecution asked you about while putting this witness's testimony to you. The date is the 12th of May, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 4, both in B/C/S and in English, so it's this document. Could the Chamber please focus on the last paragraph of the English version. And as for B/C/S, I'd ask that we move on to the fifth page, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Petrovic, this witness, five years after the statement that was put to you today, provided a statement to this Tribunal about what happened, and this is what he says. Once I've read out the relevant part, I'm going to put a few questions to you. "We waited at the roadblock at Konjevici. A UN APC driven by Serb soldiers arrived there and offered to take us to Potocari. Instead of taking us to Potocari, the Serb soldiers in the UN APC drove us in the woods near by Konjevic; thereafter, they dropped us at the roadblock. We were still at Konjevic when a UN Mercedes, driven by our fellow soldiers, came over there. They picked us and drove in the direction of Nova Kasaba." Now this kind of testimony about what happened, is this closer to your own recollection about how things developed in relation to these two members of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: We waited at the roadblock. We did not drive them to Potocari and we did not offer that. We were just told that they'd be taken for a 2-kilometre ride over there and then come back. No mention of Potocari and they never asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. The next thing that is stated here is: "Instead of taking us to Potocari, the Serb soldiers in a UN APC drove us in the woods near Konjevici." Now my question: This part of the road from Konjevic towards Bratunac, is it wooded? Are there woods on both sides?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, well, there are more houses now. I mean, more houses were built by now. But on the left and right-hand side, there was a woodland and -- do you understand what I'm saying? But there was just this road that we took. There was just that one road that we drove on and I’m saying for sure, 100 per cent, that we did not go off that road at all, and we took that same road back. We did not take any macadam road, and there was no asphalt then, that would go off this road…

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've been told by my colleague, did you say that it was macadam or not asphalt? What was it that you said?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mean what I said just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: The road that we took as we were moving in the UN vehicle, it was an asphalt road for 2 kilometres, up and down. So I just said that -- I mean, during the bombing, then there were mines, and this and that and the other thing, the road was not good. It wasn't good asphalt, not like over here now, when the situation is normal. So the road was damaged. Macadam? No, we did not take any macadam roads left or right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are recorded as having said: "Macadam, there was no asphalt then ..." Would you like us to verify that in the audio whether that is what you said or not? We'd gladly do so because we don't want to have any wrong recording of your words, but you're recorded until now as having said: "Macadam, there was no asphalt then ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, go ahead. Verify. But I mean, I don't know. I mean, that's my opinion, that there was asphalt. There's asphalt to this day. I mean, verify it. Let's see what it was that I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but did you use the word "macadam"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I said it just like I said it just now, that the road was not good, so I did not express myself well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. And there's one other question. You said you were ordered to take them for 2 kilometres. That is -- let me read it then. "We were just told that they'd be taken for a 2-kilometre ride over there and then come back." Who told you to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nikolic told us, Mr. Nikolic told us that we take these two men from the UN to where they want to go and that they should return when they want. And we went for 2 kilometres roughly and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what you just said. You just said: "We were just told that they'd be taken for a 2-kilometre ride over there and then come back." That's different from what you now say; that is, that you'd take them wherever they wanted to go and that they insisted on returning. You said a minute ago that you were ordered to take them to a 2-kilometre drive and then come back. Have you any explanation as for the -- the difference in what you told us earlier and now again and what you said about being instructed to take them for a 2-kilometre ride? No -- no speaking aloud. Mr. Mladic. No speaking aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't explain it any other way. That's what I meant every time, when I was speaking. Now, I mean, they should be driven for 2 kilometres -- it's not that the order given to me was that they should be driven for 2 kilometres. Mr. Nikolic said the soldiers should be taken for as long as they want and then we drove them those 2 kilometres and then they wanted to come back and we brought them back. That's what I've been saying all along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they would not have told you after 2 kilometres to return, what would have happened? You would just have been driven on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what we were told. For as long as they want to go, for as far as they want to go, that we should drive them to there. Had they wanted 1 kilometre, it would have been 1; had they wanted 3, then it would have been 3. We would have done that and returned them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10 kilometres you would done as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, also. Because that's what we were told. We were told to drive them for as long as they wanted. We weren't told a specific number of kilometres, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to us again what was the purpose of that, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. It's probably they who know what they wanted. I cannot remember any of that, that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean by "they," UN; or do you mean by "they," Nikolic and others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Nikolic and the UN soldiers. They should know. I mean, what they wanted. Why they wanted to take that road. Unless they reached some kind of agreement beforehand with Nikolic. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question related to this text. The witness says that upon returning to Konjevic - you can see that in front of you: "A UN Mercedes arrived driven by our fellow soldiers ... they picked them up and drove them in the direction of Nova Kasaba." This part of this testimony, does this correspond to your own recollection; namely, that they took a different UN vehicle and left Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say for sure now whether it was a Mercedes. Do you understand that? But they did take some vehicle, yes. Now whether it was a Mercedes, I didn't understand. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of you give them any kind of trouble? Did you try to prevent them in any way from leaving the APC and, after that, Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no one, nothing. They did whatever it was that they wanted to do. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm going to conclude with the following question: On that day, did you have any conflict with any of the members of UN or UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I did not have a conflict with anyone, not with the soldiers, not with those who were being taken prisoner there. No one. No one. That's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those days, or on that day, did you have the opportunity of seeing General Mladic anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that day, no, not before that, not after that. I personally did not have an opportunity to meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I shall conclude with the following question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, that's now the second time that you say that the following question will conclude your examination. But I take it that you're serious now and it's not in five or six questions from now that you will conclude. So we'll listen to your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. I will conclude with this last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, tell us, after those few days, except for the 14th which you discussed already, did you at any point use that APC?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, except for that time when we were the escort to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, if I may, just arising from Your Honours' questions of the witness regarding the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have Exhibit P10 -- sorry, P01539 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Before this comes up, you can help us with this. There were smaller roads, weren't there, going off the main road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were macadam roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Page 21, please. There we are. Page 21. And if we could just enlarge it, I think it might help if we enlarge it a bit around the second -- the middle of the -- the road in effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want the road or the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The map enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we could look at the map only to start with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, that would be better. Thank you, Your Honour. That I think is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is a map of part of the road from Konjevic Polje, which you can see -- you can't see it on the map but it's up in the north-west of road going all the way to Bratunac. That what's this map shows. You agree with that; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And to the south of this road, these were the woods from which the Muslim men were coming down onto this main road here, going towards Konjevic Polje; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you can see, just to get our locations right, in the middle of this road here with all this -- the markings on it, which makes it a little bit difficult to see, but by the number 17a, right in the middle of that -- right at the top of that square, reads Sandici, so you can see that just there, to the north of this road there on the map is Sandici; yes? Just to get our locations clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, I'm trying to find it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, it's the right -- it's written over, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: 17a is written over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What is confusing here is that, of course, on the small map there is a 17a as well but no Sandici next to it, so you should focus on the large map and where it's written 17a, so not the small extract but the large map, larger -- covering the larger area. Do you see at 17a Sandici just written below it, under it, Witness? Can you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see it. I see Lolici.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Looking on the road from Lolici going east --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: To the right. And then when you get to the red box, look slightly north of the red box, and Sandici is written there. It's covered up a little bit by the number 17 but there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's where the cursor is at this moment. You see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, this thing up here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. You can see below the road there a number of smaller roads going off the main road just to the south of the road at Sandici; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not really an expert. I can't find my way around here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: But let me help you with this. To the south of the road, the main road, there are some smaller roads, and one of them goes to Kamenica, and you can see Kamenica there at the very bottom of this map in the middle. Kamenica almost directly in the middle but in the -- in the bottom rows. The cursor is on it now. Got it?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. There is a road going from the main road to Kamenica, it's one of the smaller roads off the main roads; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I see the road here, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yup. Now we go back up to -- onto the main road, please, and we're going to drive up to Konjevic Polje, to the intersection, so we go up leftwards, north-west along this road, and we get to another road after --

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- Lolici. Can you see there's another road after Lolici, and it's in the second square -- from the left, second square down. Full square down. There's another road where it says Kravica. There's a road to the south of the main road -- yes, got it? Perhaps the cursor could find it. It's going up leftwards up the road --

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Lolici are here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Past Kravica, there's a -- the cursor was absolutely right. It was where it says Kravica, there is a road that -- another road to the south of the main road. And that was absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Lolici are here, Kravica is here --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, it's actually the -- it's actually where the cursor is now. It's a river. That's what that reading of Kravica is. Okay. And you can see a road just next to it right off the main road. Got it? Yes? Where the cursor is.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This road goes to Burnice, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It goes --

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: But I don't know these things. I don't know where they.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This road, which goes to Burnice, is accessible via an APC, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't take that road. I can't even remember now whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please come to your point, Ms. Pack, what you intend to demonstrate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm showing you a road off the main road which an APC is capable of travelling down. This could have been the road you went up with those Dutch soldiers, right, in the APC? You would accept that? Not saying it is but it's one of the roads off the main road?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the parties can agree on that, I mean, that there are roads off the main road and, of course, that if the witness is not telling us the truth, that he stayed on the main road. That that could have been one of the roads, of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is argument rather than anything else. It doesn't bring us to the facts. The witness says, I didn't go on those roads, I don't know whether you could drive with an APC on that. The parties can agree or disagree or you can present whatever evidence, but this is not -- it doesn't bring us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've leave it there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Bench also has no further questions, Mr. Petrovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, were put to you by the parties, were put to you by the Bench, and I would invite to you follow the usher, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the next witness be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: With Your Honours' permission, may I leave the court. My friend Mr. Traldi [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that the Srebrenica team -- when we're leaving Srebrenica, that the Srebrenica team is leaving as well. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of course you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Javoric. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Javoric. Mr. Javoric, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, would you tell us slowly your full name.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Rade Javoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Javoric, have you given a statement to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've given a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1D1697 on our screens, please. And we need paragraph 30 on our screens. It's on page -- second-last page of the both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Javoric, during proofing you told me that in this paragraph the first sentence was not properly recorded. I'll read the sentence out in English so the parties can follow. [In English] Paragraph 30 from the statement reads, I quote: "I would say that by refusing to respond to the mobilisation call, the Muslims and the Croats contributed to the creation of ethnically clean units." And you corrected this and you told me that this sentence should read as follows: "I would say that by refusing to respond to the mobilisation call, some Muslims and Croats contributed to the imbalance of ethnic composition of units."

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Precisely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now that we've made this correction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then suggest that at the end of paragraph 30 that a correction should be made as well. I read the last line to you: "Therefore, the places that had to be filled because the Muslims and the Croats had not responded were filled by the Serbs." Should that then read: "Therefore, the places that had to be filled because some Muslims and some Croats had not responded were filled by the Serbs who responded to the mobilisation call"? Should we make that correction as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can say, but I think it's understood from the first sentence he was already talking about some Muslims and some Croats, but if you deem it better I [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm just wondering why only in half the paragraph the language should be changed and whereas we leave the same language at a later stage unaffected. That's my concern. That if you start with some and later say "the Muslims" and "the Croats," that may confuse. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It certainly might confuse me, Your Honour. But I'd just ask that two things be clarified. First, with -- with the witness. First, as Your Honour suggested, whether the witness's evidence is that some Muslims and Croats responded to the mobilisation, because I would suggest that's distinct from any that might have been in the units beforehand. Second, as there are multiple mobilisations during the time period that the witness is talking about, I'd ask that we get a clarification as to which one is being discussed in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, would it not be best to resolve these matters right in the beginning so that we know exactly what we are admitting --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if we are -- if would you tendered the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now being aware that it can -- might create confusion, then we would -- according to your instructions, we would correct the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, correct -- I think as a matter of fact, that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and then I would proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wondered whether we would have to correct that as well, because the same language is used there in the same context. And the second issue is that Mr. Traldi --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would like to have this clarified. But, Mr. Traldi, may I take it that if Mr. Lukic considers your concerns clear enough that you would deal with the matter in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I suppose, though I would think that type of ambiguity is most easily addressed before admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's a suggestion and we'll see whether Mr. Lukic will follow that. Then, Witness, the last sentence, and you have it in front of you: "Therefore, the places that had to be filled because the Muslims and the Croats had not responded were filled by the Serbs." Do you want to change that as well in "some Muslims" and "some Croats," or would you rather keep it as it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be changed in order to be clearer. Later on I will describe the situation as it was in the initial days of the mobilisation, in the initial stage of the mobilisation, because there were several mobilisation drives, and why the Croats and Muslims did not respond any longer as they had in the past. And then I will come to the resulting ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Likely some questions will be put to you in this respect. With this understanding, I take it that you want to tender the document, Mr. Lukic, after you have asked further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Should I clarify the mobilisations first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave that to you, whether you want to do it now or whether you would do it later once you have tendered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I'll proceed with the attestation and then after that clarify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Javoric, after we've made these corrections to paragraph 30, is the remaining part of your statement recorded properly? Is it exactly what you said to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you presented as your knowledge in this statement, is it truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I were to put to you the same questions today, would you substantially answer the same?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, now we would tender the statement of Mr. Javoric, 1D1697, into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01697 receives Exhibit D895, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D895 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave I would read short statement summary and then proceed with some questions. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can I just ask one clarification for the record beforehand from Mr. Lukic. When Mr. Lukic asked about what the witness was presenting as his knowledge, was he asking about the entire statement or just the parts that purport to reflect firsthand knowledge? And I'm looking at page 76, lines 16 through 18 of the temporary transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. It is in the transcript maybe not clear, but I think in -- my B/C/S question was a bit more clear, but I can repeat it or I can say that I tried to attest the whole statement and my question was directed toward the whole statement not only toward the paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I appreciate the clarification and that answers the question I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see another ambiguity. When you asked if the witness would answer in the same way if the same questions are put to him, he said: "Yes, for the most part." And what about the other part? Perhaps you can clarify that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Javoric, what did you mean when you said in your previous answer "for the most part"?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: When I said "for the most part," I meant that now I would provide much broader and more detailed and more complete explanations and answers than I did before, because I answered questions from my own standpoint as a professional and I used a lot of terms and maybe jargon that may not be understandable to all. I will, through my answers, provide more detailed, more specific information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Javoric. I believe we've clarified everything now. I'll now read a short summary of your statement and then I'll put a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Rade Javoric will speak about the situation in Prijedor before, during, and after the multi-party elections. He will explain ethnic composition of the Territorial Defence Staff of Prijedor and its units. He was appointed commander of the Prijedor Territorial Defence Staff on 16th of September, 1991, and he held this position when the war in B and H started. Mr. Javoric will testify about military units present in Prijedor area. Mr. Javoric will testify about the system of command and control over TO units. Mr. Javoric will also testify about the mobilisation processes and about the failure of Muslims and Croats to respond to the call to the war units. He will testify that everyone who responded to the mobilisation call received equipment, weapons, and ammunition. He will present information about the preparation of the Muslims for the war in the territory of the municipality; about his encounter with an armed and uniformed member -- members of the Muslim Territorial Defence at Kozarac village in May 1992; about the blocking of the regional road Banja Luka-Prijedor at Kozarac; about the start of war in Prijedor with the murder of two soldiers by Muslim forces at the Hambarine village check-point; and about other events that took place that same period. And that was the statement summary, Your Honours. And with your leave, I would put several questions to Mr. Javoric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how much time you would need for that? Because we had the last break we had rather late, and in order to avoid that we have only a last session of five or ten minutes, I'm wondering. But could you tell us how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will need the rest of the day and probably some time tomorrow, Your Honours. I asked for one hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that we take the break now so that you have an uninterrupted last half an hour for your ... Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'd just like to briefly comment the matter which was raised by the parties, that the witness attesting to what is his own knowledge to be true. Of course, that's part of hearsay. If there's hearsay evidence in the statement, then of course the witness can attest to what he heard, not necessarily to the truth of what he heard. So in that respect, I think Mr. Lukic rightly phrased it as he did. At the same time, Mr. Lukic, if, for example, we look at paragraph 26, sometimes it's totally unclear whether it's hearsay or not. It's a very short paragraph. It reads: "I claim that the military did not secure investigation and collection centres in and around Prijedor." Now, it's totally unclear whether this is hearsay or whether this is personal knowledge because no basis for it has been established. So therefore to some extent you are right, in view of the hearsay, to ask for what the witness observed himself. At the same time, you create a problem by using this kind of language in the statement. We take a break and we'll resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber noticed that in relation to the testimony of the previous witness that there were two items where there was some discussion about what the witness exactly had said. It was put to him how it was recorded. The Chamber would very much like to verify whether the expression "not a proper road" was really used by the witness, and the same for the macadam road, so that we know for sure what the witness has said. And of course, we invited him several times to explain and to verify and to tell us if he did not agree. So therefore, those two specific expressions recorded as having been used by the witness, the Chamber would like to have it verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will give later the lines. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Javoric, you'll now be further examined by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would need assistance from the usher to give the statement of Mr. Javoric to him. Can you give the Prosecution to check it. Since I'll go through several paragraphs from that statement, I would like Mr. Javoric to check the statement while we are talking about the paragraphs. And on our screens, we need paragraph 6. It's page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Javoric, we need paragraph 6. Would you like to find it? Have you opened it?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record and for the clarity of the statement, you mentioned a few names here, and I'm just going ask you something about these persons that you said were members of the Territorial Defence Staff. You mentioned Aziz Selimbegovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was Mr. Selimbegovic's ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: His rank was of that a major and his ethnicity was Muslim and it was a very important post on my staff where I was commander. Should I explain what it was that he did?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please listen to my question and then just answer questions. We'll go through all of this. You said that it was an important post, the one that he held. What was he in charge of in your Territorial Defence staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: I have to say that the TO Staff functioned according to JNA rules, and the commander has his assistant commanders and the Chief of Staff has his own assistant chiefs. Selimbegovic was assistant chief of the TO for logistics, an exceptionally important position because as assistant for logistics he had within his domain people who were in charge of weaponry, ammunition, medicine, equipment; so the chief of the medical corps, the chief of the veterinary service, the chief of the technical service, and not to enumerate all of them. So this is a person that was in the focus of all of these activities. He had his subordinates, he commanded them, and he informed the commander about everything they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next name mentioned is a Iso Bucan. Mr. Bucan, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Iso Bucan was a Muslim. He had a university degree, a very important post on the staff. He was chief of security, and he received instructions from the District Staff; that is to say, instructions, rules, and we who were lower-ranking did not have that kind of opportunity to communicate with superiors as he did. He finished different schools and he held a responsible position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Javoric, soon you will be cautioned by the Court to answer the questions that are put to you. I asked what you his ethnicity was and the answer was Muslim. And then we would elaborate further. Vahid Ceric, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his task?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Vahid Ceric was assistant Chief of Staff for organisational and personnel affairs. This is a position of exceptional importance; that is to say, Vahid Ceric assigned officers to different posts and he would receive the names from the municipal department. He had an assistant of his own, his name was Milenko Kostic. So all the personnel that were deployed in the TO, and later I guess that we will be talking about the units there, he was responsible for that, and he made proposals to the commander and then the commander would make proposals to the council and then the council would take all of that into account and make their decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say council, what council?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: The Council for National Defence in the municipality was in charge of personnel affairs as far as units in the field are concerned. As far as operational units are concerned, including the 5th Brigade, that was done by the council of the republic staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic announced well that soon the Court would tell you to focus your answer on the questions. That is, what council? The Council for National Defence in the municipality. That's the answer to the question. What their duty was, what they did, et cetera, if Mr. Lukic is interested in knowing that, he'll ask you. So please focus your answer on what is asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Vahid Ceric assigned officers to different units. Who assigned soldiers to different units and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Also Mr. Vahid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain to us from your point of view as a professional on the Territorial Defence Staff what is the legal requirement for manning units and for providing technical equipment to them?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: According to establishment, units have to be 100 per cent manned and equipped and there should be a certain reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next person mentioned in this paragraph is Kemal Terzic. Mr. Terzic, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was stated that he was an operations officer together with Mr. Vlado Mool. Let me ask you first what the ethnicity of Vlado Mool is?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Vlado Mool is an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does that mean, that they were operations personnel? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: They were in charge of carrying out professional military training; that is to say, for infantry and certain specialist courses. And they were trained to do that. The third operations person was Rajko Macura. So there were three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Goran Bikic is also mentioned. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that an order had arrived for you to be moved to the barracks and people had to sign up in terms of whether they wanted to or not, and you said that Mr. Vahid Ceric did not sign that and was not transferred there. Bucan, Iso, did not sign it but he did transfer to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Iso Bucan, did he have any problems because he did not sign and he had transferred nevertheless?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did not have any problems. He said that he didn't want to sign anything because he had already taken an oath in the JNA, so he transferred there and continued working on intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we've come to the topic that was raised at the very beginning of your testimony. Please take a look at paragraph 8 of your statement. It has to do with mobilisation. And in that paragraph, you tell us that the TO Staff issued an order to the TO Staff to the Prijedor National Defence Secretariat to mobilise people and MTS by formation. First explain this to us, the difference between operative and territorial units within the Territorial Defence so that we could distinguish between these different structures.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: On the Territorial Defence staff there was the 5th Kozara Brigade. It was an operative unit. It was not linked to a particular territory. Our task was to equip it, mobilise it, and hand it over to the Republican Staff. Do you want me to continue? In addition to the 5th Brigade in the Territorial Defence Staff, there was also the sabotage reconnaissance unit that was a platoon consisting of individuals who had particular specialities. In addition to that, there was the Dr. Mladen Stojanovic Detachment. It was at battalion level. Then the logistics company in the staff. And many units in the territory, I shall explain, in local communes, and in companies. Forty-eight units in local communes and companies. These units, in terms of their purpose and task, could not leave the territory. Rather, they were supposed to secure different facilities within the municipality. For example, factories. For example, we have a biscuit factory there in Prijedor and it works on gas, and their task was to provide gas. And then also the waterworks, that provided water to the entire town. And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who decides that mobilisation should be carried out and the people should be mobilised into the 5th Kozara Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: We receive an order from the District Staff and the District Staff receives an order from the republic staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who makes a decision to mobilise people into local units in local communes and companies?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: The Council for National Defence of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in practice, when the National Defence Council of the municipality of Prijedor reaches such a decision, who do they address?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: The council sends this conclusion of theirs to the staff. As far as territorial units are concerned, they are commanded by the Territorial Defence Staff, and then we send it to the Secretary for National Defence. Perhaps this is not a very nice term that I'm going to use now, but they acted as a kind of service station for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is it that they do for you by way of providing services?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: So we have reached the question of mobilisation and call-up. In the staff there is establishment, and according to establishment a unit has to be manned and equipped. In the secretariat, there is a courier service that in peacetime it received training several times, and for each and every unit they have their own couriers and for all directions. When we send an order and we say that a unit, 1516/3 should be mobilised, that is a code, and over there at the National Defence they know which unit this is. Then they activate the courier service and they send call-up papers for the entire unit. According to priority, first of all, it is the officers in the unit that receive call-up papers and they are the first to report at the mobilisation site. Afterwards, there is direct security for this unit, and at the same time materiel and technical equipment is taken from the barracks. So all weapons for that unit, side-arms, equipment, armour, food, medicine, all of that is sent to the mobilisation site. Once the couriers return, they provide papers to the staff, and then Vahid Ceric from the staff goes to the mobilisation site and reports to the commander saying how many people responded to call-up. Those who do show up are issued with weapons on basis of their files. Some get an automatic rifle, others get a mortar, others get a submachine-gun, and so on. So those who respond to call-up get weapons, equipment, and everything else that is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are talking about mobilisation from 1992, as far as I understand you; is that right? September 1991, sorry. 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Did you receive visits after mobilisation had been carried out? Visits from superior commands, that is.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We were visited by General Jakic, Fikret Jakic, the head of the Republic Staff for Territorial Defence. He first visited me, he asked me what the situation was like, and then we went to see the president of the municipality, and there we reported to him about what the situation was like in terms of mobilisation, call-up, response. There were pressures there by national units that interfered in the work of the command, the work of the staff, but we who were there did not allow them to play a part there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Javoric, you said - and it was interpreted that way - that there were pressures by national or ethnic units. Did you mean national parties?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: National parties. And later, it turned out, unfortunately, that they -- these parties had formed some of their own paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was just asking you about the units part.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: No, I meant the leaders of these national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fikret Jakic, general. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Muslim. Chief of the republic staff of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, what was his stance on the mobilisation? Was it necessary to carry it out, not necessary, or necessary to partially carry it out? What was his stand?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: It was the correct stance. According to the rules of the republic staff, he said it had to be done and that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The two of you went to brief the president of the municipality. What was his ethnicity and what was his name, the president of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. He taught the Serbo-Croat language.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can't remember the name?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: It alludes me for the moment but I'll remember. We sat down over coffee so many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Except in the office of the president of the municipality, was the mobilisation discussed in political organisations, bodies of Prijedor? Did you inform political parties about the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The greatest pressure was exerted by the SDA and the SDS, whereas Croats and their national leaders were the most moderate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us -- in fact, what did you say in these briefings to the SDS, for instance?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC
utterances.text: We told them the truth. Namely, on the 24th of September, 1991, I went to Omarska to emphasise -- and its 100 per cent Serb population, the SDS was the strongest there, and I took Vahid Ceric with me. Vahid Ceric was the chief of training and mobilisation. I remember those figures. We drafted 650 Serbs, 550 Muslims, and 87 Croats. Later on, I experienced some unpleasantness from members of the SDS. They criticised me. How come you brought Vahid as one of the commanders and you came to the SDS headquarters? I always acted like that wherever I was going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked what you said in those briefings. You go far beyond that. Apart from that, it's time to adjourn for the day, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. And I instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever it may be about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that's clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before we adjourn, I'd like to clarify that the portions of the transcript of today's provisional transcript to be verified are on page 46, line 12, where the witness was recorded as having said "not a proper road," and page 62, line 13 to 14, where the witness came up with the word "macadam." We'd like to know -- it's unclear whether the witness said, I didn't say it or not, he was rather vague about that. But the Chamber wants to be sure that if this is what he said -- if it's not what he said, that we have to consider that and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tried, even at that moment, to consult with Mr. Stojanovic, and we couldn't recall really properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's the reason why I would like this to be verified on the basis of the audio so that there should be no doubt as to whether the witness, who was questioned on these words in some detail, whether he spoke those words, yes or no. That's the page and line references are there now. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 10th of February, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
